newsitem.title: JAPAN: Alumax CEO sees firmer 1997 aluminium price.
newsitem.headline: Alumax CEO sees firmer 1997 aluminium price.

text.p: A drawdown in inventories should boost aluminium prices in the first half of 1997, Alumax Inc chief executive Allen Born said on Tuesday.

"We're going to get away from the excess inventory picture. We should see a more normal supply-and-demand curve and when that happens we should have a little bit better pricing," he told Reuters in an interview.
"Don't get too excited for the last quarter (of 1996)," he added. "Going into the first and second quarter of next year I think you'll see some improvement."
He added that the firmer prices should help Alumax's bottom line. "Any time you get a better price you're going to have a better income picture," he said.
The company last month reported a year-on-year decline in operating profits for the third quarter of this year, due in large part to softer aluminium prices.
Born also blamed speculation on the London Metal Exchange for knocking aluminium prices out of line with market fundamentals over the past eight months.

"When it (the market) is lacklustre I think people back away from LME and some of the other speculators get in, and when this happens you really get a false feeling of what that market is," he said. "I think that's what we've been going through for the last eight months."
The price of benchmark LME three-month aluminium has fallen steadily since May, reaching a 2-1/2-year low of $1,305 a tonne on October 10.
LME prices have since rebounded somewhat, ending Monday's afternoon kerb at $1,424.50 a tonne.
Born said steady gains in demand would help fuel a drawdown in inventories.
"The demand we are seeing in our order books is not bad, and when that happens and when you can see there's an inventory drawdown you're going to have better prices," he said.
He said rising consumption should absorb an expected 243,000-tonne rise in worldwide production next year.
He added that, despite the recent drop in LME prices, he saw no reason to resurrect the 1994 Memorandum of Understanding that limited aluminium production.
"I see no logic in it whatsoever," he said.
The memorandum, signed in early 1994 by the governments of several aluminium producing countries to help address a supply glut, expired early this year.
